title: What Venom Has Actually Given Medicine
topic: venom as a source of medicines
paragraphs: Every few years a headline announces that the next great painkiller is swimming in a tide pool or coiled under a rock.
Venom is chemistry built to shut down a nervous system or a circulatory system in seconds, and the molecules that do it are extraordinarily good at their jobs.
Researchers like to call venom a library that evolution has already screened against the very proteins medicine wants to control.
The premise is sound.
The output is thin.
After five decades of effort, the list of approved drugs that trace back to venom is short enough to recite from memory.
The first thing to correct is the singular noun: there is no such thing as the toxin in a snake or a scorpion.

A venom is a mixture of dozens to hundreds of components: enzymes that break down tissue, salts and small molecules that cause pain and swelling, and, of most interest to drug developers, short folded peptides that bind ion channels and receptors.
Cone snails are the extreme case.
More than seven hundred species are known, one species may produce well over a hundred peptides, and the mixture shifts depending on whether the animal is hunting or defending.
The components are not redundant: some paralyze, some block escape reflexes, and several do little alone and much together.
The peptides are small, usually ten to forty amino acids.
What makes them durable is not length but stitching.
Cysteine residues along the chain pair off into disulfide bonds that lash distant parts of the sequence together.
In one common arrangement, the inhibitor cystine knot, three such bonds build a compact core in which one bond threads through the ring formed by the other two.
The result behaves less like a floppy string than like a bead of hardened resin, resistant to heat, to acid, and to the enzymes that destroy ordinary peptides.
That rigid core explains the selectivity that first drew pharmacologists in.
The cysteines and the fold they create stay conserved; the residues on the loops between them do not.
Venom genes duplicate readily, and the copies accumulate changes on the exposed surface while the skeleton holds still.
Prey evolve resistance, predators need fresh keys, and the cycle repeats.
What comes out is a set of peptides that can tell nearly identical proteins apart.
Nearly identical is not an exaggeration.

Humans carry nine subtypes of voltage-gated sodium channel, built alike and sharing much of their sequence, yet sitting in different tissues: one in a pain-sensing nerve, one in heart muscle, one in skeletal muscle.
A drug that blocks all of them stops the heart.
Chemists have spent decades trying to build small molecules that touch one subtype and spare the rest, with limited success, because the pockets they bind are so alike.
Venom peptides sidestep that by not using a pocket.
They lie across the outer face of the channel and read a patch of its surface, and small differences there decide whether the peptide sticks.
Here the story usually stops being told carefully.
Binding tightly to a human channel is a laboratory result, not a therapy, and the distance between them is where nearly every venom program has died.
It helps to ask what the animal was selecting for.
A predator needs a dose delivered by needle into tissue, acting within seconds, on an animal it will eat and never see again.
Nothing pressed it toward a molecule safe at a steady dose for six months, able to survive a stomach, or careful with the one tissue a patient cannot lose.
Evolution screened for the predator's problem.
The patient's problem was never on the test.
The practical form of that mismatch is the window.
Every drug has a range between the amount that helps and the amount that harms, and a compound's usefulness depends far more on the width of that range than on its strength at the low end.
Venom peptides tend to have narrow ones.
A molecule bred to be lethal at vanishingly small concentrations does not become gentle once purified and named.
Several candidates worked as designed in patients and were dropped anyway, because the dose that eased symptoms sat close to the dose that brought dizziness, confusion, or a fall in blood pressure.
Against that, the record of approved drugs is short but real.
Captopril reached patients in 1981 as the first approved drug to block angiotensin converting enzyme.
It began with peptides in a Brazilian pit viper's venom that lowered blood pressure by prolonging a signaling molecule the enzyme destroys.
Chemists did not develop the peptide; they worked out how it met the enzyme, then built a small molecule that met it the same way and could be swallowed.

Eptifibatide, approved in 1998, is a seven-residue ring modeled on a rattlesnake venom protein that keeps platelets from clumping; tirofiban, cleared the same year, hits the same target with a synthetic molecule of similar shape.

Exenatide, approved in 2005, is a thirty-nine residue peptide from the saliva of the Gila monster; it lowers blood sugar through the same receptor as a human hormone whose natural half-life is about two minutes, and because the lizard version resists the enzyme that clips the human one, it lasts for hours.
The purest case is ziconotide, a twenty-five residue peptide with three disulfide bonds, identical to one made by a fish-hunting cone snail.
It blocks a calcium channel on the spinal neurons that relay pain upward.
Approved in the United States in 2004, it eases pain when opioids have failed.
It is also close to unusable.
Swallowed, it is destroyed.
In a vein, it is filtered out by the kidney within minutes, and it could not cross into the central nervous system anyway.
The only route that works is continuous infusion through a catheter threaded into the fluid around the spinal cord, fed by a pump implanted under the skin.
Even then the window is narrow enough that the dose must be raised slowly over weeks.
So the tally is roughly a dozen, most of them injected, and several not peptides at all but small molecules designed after a peptide showed the way.
Set that against the pool.
More than two hundred thousand animal species are thought to be venomous, and the number of distinct venom peptides has been put in the millions.
Well under one percent have ever been tested against a human target.
Both halves of that comparison get quoted, usually to argue that a breakthrough is near.
The same numbers read the other way: an enormous input has produced a small output, and the reasons are not mysterious.
Most of those reasons concern getting the molecule where it must go.
A peptide taken by mouth meets stomach acid and then a wall of digestive enzymes, and whatever survives is too large and too polar to cross the gut lining.
Injection solves that and creates a second problem: small peptides slip through the filter in the kidney and are gone from the blood in minutes.
Targets inside the brain or spinal cord sit behind a barrier peptides do not cross.
Any foreign sequence may also be recognized by the immune system, which can neutralize the drug or attack the patient's own tissue.
None of these are failures of potency.
There is a tool for each problem, which is why the field has not given up.
A peptide can be closed into a ring, hung with a chain of polyethylene glycol, or rebuilt from mirror-image amino acids, each change buying time against the enzymes or the kidney.
Each change also alters the surface that made the peptide selective, so the rebuilt molecule often has to prove itself again.
It is worth being blunt about the framing that keeps the field oversold.
Calling venom a library is a metaphor doing a great deal of unearned work.
A library implies that the hard part, generating good candidates, is finished, and that what remains is retrieval.
What evolution supplied is a very large set of molecules optimized for an unrelated purpose, in which a handful happen to be useful and there is no index.
Counting sequences is not counting leads.
The gap between a peptide that exists and one that can be given to a patient is where the work lives, and being natural does not narrow it.
The technical picture has changed far more than the clinical one.

For most of the twentieth century the limit was supply: a researcher milked animals, separated the pooled venom by chromatography, tested the fractions in a bioassay, and needed a great deal of raw material to isolate a usable quantity of one component.
Sequencing the venom gland changed that: reading the messenger RNA there yields the sequence of everything the animal is building, including peptides far too scarce to isolate by hand.
The bottleneck moved rather than vanished.
Thousands of sequences now arrive with no indication of what any of them binds, and testing one peptide against a panel of ion channels stays slow and costly even with automated instruments.
The pain channel called Nav1.7 shows the pattern in miniature.
People born without a working copy feel no pain and are otherwise largely ordinary, which makes it about as well validated a target as exists.
Spider and scorpion venoms gave up peptides that block it with great potency, programs were funded, candidates entered trials, and the results have been repeatedly disappointing.
The channel may yet yield.
What it has not done is yield easily.
The fair summary is neither the press release nor the dismissal.

Venom has given medicine a small number of genuinely useful drugs and a much larger number of research tools: a peptide that blocks one channel subtype and nothing else is how a physiologist proves what that subtype does.

Its most reliable contribution has been information rather than product: a demonstration that a protein can be hit selectively, which chemists can then pursue with molecules that behave better in a body.
Captopril is the template, not ziconotide.
The animal did not make a drug.
It made an argument that a drug was possible, and the rest of the work belongs to people.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the only delivery route that works for ziconotide is
choices: a tablet taken by mouth on a regular daily schedule
an injection into a vein, repeated several times through the day
a steady infusion into the fluid that bathes the spinal cord
a patch worn on the skin above the part of the body that hurts
a single injection into the muscle at the site of the pain

proof.quote: continuous infusion through a catheter threaded into the fluid around the spinal cord
it is filtered out by the kidney within minutes

questions.why: Paragraph 9 walks through the routes that fail and lands on the one that works: a catheter threaded into the fluid around the spinal cord, fed by a pump implanted under the skin.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9 says that swallowed, the peptide is destroyed.
The same paragraph rules a vein out, since the kidney clears the peptide within minutes and it cannot reach the central nervous system.
No skin patch appears anywhere in the passage; the routes weighed are the mouth, a vein, and the space around the spinal cord.
A muscle injection is never mentioned, and any injection into the body still leaves the peptide facing the kidney and the barrier around the nervous system.

questions.stem: The passage says the peptide found in Gila monster saliva outlasts the human hormone it mimics because it
choices: resists the enzyme that clips the human version
binds a different and considerably more durable receptor
is far smaller than the human hormone it stands in for
is taken by mouth rather than injected into the patient
carries three disulfide bonds that hold its shape together

proof.quote: the lizard version resists the enzyme that clips the human one
through the same receptor as a human hormone

questions.why: Paragraph 8 gives the reason outright: the human hormone has a natural half-life of about two minutes, and the lizard version lasts for hours because it resists the enzyme that clips the human one.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 states that it works through the same receptor as the human hormone, not a different one.
Size is never offered as the reason, and the passage puts the peptide at thirty-nine residues without comparing it to the hormone.
Nothing says this drug is swallowed, and paragraph 10 notes that most venom-derived drugs are injected.
Three disulfide bonds belong to ziconotide in paragraph 9, not to the peptide from the lizard.

questions.stem: As the passage describes it, the inhibitor cystine knot consists of
choices: a single disulfide bond looping the two ends of the chain together
three disulfide bonds lying side by side along the outer surface of the peptide
a ring of cysteines that grips the ion channel directly
three disulfide bonds, one threaded through the ring made by the other two
a knot of hydrogen bonds formed between neighboring amino acids

proof.quote: one bond threads through the ring formed by the other two

questions.why: Paragraph 3 defines the arrangement exactly: three disulfide bonds build a compact core, and one of them threads through the ring formed by the other two.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 describes three bonds in this arrangement, not one.
The number is right and the geometry is not, since one bond passes through the ring the other two make.
The cysteines hold the peptide's own shape in paragraph 3; the surface that meets a channel is described in paragraph 5.
Paragraph 3 names disulfide bonds between cysteine residues, not hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: The passage attributes the trouble chemists have had in targeting a single sodium channel subtype to
choices: the small number of subtypes they have available to work with
the close similarity of the pockets that small molecules bind
the barrier that keeps drugs out of the brain and spinal cord
the speed with which the body clears small molecules from the blood
the immune response that a foreign molecule provokes in the patient

proof.quote: because the pockets they bind are so alike

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says chemists have had limited success because the pockets those molecules bind are so alike from one subtype to the next.
distractorNotes: Nine subtypes is a fact from paragraph 5, but their number is never treated as the obstacle.
That barrier is a peptide delivery problem in paragraph 11, not the reason a small molecule cannot single out one subtype.
Rapid clearance in paragraph 11 applies to small peptides in the kidney, and it is a dosing problem rather than a targeting one.
Immune recognition appears in paragraph 11 as a hazard for foreign sequences, not as the reason subtypes are hard to tell apart.

questions.stem: According to the passage, sequencing the venom gland made it possible to obtain
choices: a finished drug with no further chemistry required of anyone
a reliable prediction of which channel each peptide will block
a short and manageable list of the most promising candidates
a way to test many peptides at once against a panel of channels
the sequences of peptides too scarce to isolate by hand

proof.quote: including peptides far too scarce to isolate by hand
with no indication of what any of them binds
stays slow and costly even with automated instruments

questions.why: Paragraph 14 says that reading the gland's messenger RNA yields the sequence of everything the animal is building, including peptides far too scarce to isolate by hand.
distractorNotes: The same paragraph says the bottleneck moved rather than vanished, and a sequence still has to be made and tested.
Paragraph 14 says the opposite, that thousands of sequences arrive with no indication of what any of them binds.
Sequencing produced thousands of candidates, which paragraph 14 presents as the new problem rather than a solution.
Testing against a panel of ion channels is called slow and costly in paragraph 14, even with automated instruments.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, "window" most nearly means
choices: the span between a dose that helps and a dose that harms
the period during which a drug stays active inside the body
the opening in a channel through which a peptide passes
the brief chance a research team has to publish a finding
the range of patients for whom a treatment has been approved

proof.quote: a range between the amount that helps and the amount that harms
The practical form of that mismatch is the window.

questions.why: Paragraph 7 defines the term as it goes: every drug has a range between the amount that helps and the amount that harms, and venom peptides tend to have narrow ones.
distractorNotes: A stretch of time is the everyday sense of the word, but paragraph 7 is measuring amounts of drug rather than hours.
Paragraph 5 has peptides lying across a channel's outer face rather than passing through an opening, and paragraph 7 is about dosing.
Nothing in the passage concerns publishing; the paragraph is about the gap between a helpful dose and a harmful one.
Which patients may receive a drug never comes up in paragraph 7, which is about how much of it is safe to give.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 13, "library" most nearly means
choices: a place where research findings are stored and looked up
an orderly record of every venom peptide yet reported
a ready stock of candidate molecules to be drawn on
a set of instructions an organism follows to build a protein
a collection of research tools kept on hand for teaching

proof.quote: generating good candidates, is finished, and that what remains is retrieval
a library that evolution has already screened

questions.why: Paragraph 13 takes the word apart as the field uses it: a library implies that good candidates have already been generated and that what remains is retrieval, which is what a waiting stock of compounds would mean.
distractorNotes: That is the everyday sense, and the author's complaint is precisely that venom is not a place where usable answers sit waiting.
An orderly record is the part the author denies, since the same paragraph says there is no index.
The passage never uses the word for genetic instructions; the metaphor concerns a supply of compounds.
Research tools do appear in paragraph 16, but the metaphor in paragraph 13 is about candidate drugs, not teaching.

questions.stem: The account of captopril and tirofiban in paragraph 8 most strongly supports which conclusion?
choices: Most of the drugs that trace back to venom can be taken by mouth.
A venom molecule can lead to a medicine containing none of the venom.
Small molecules reach targets that venom peptides are unable to reach.
Peptides are on the whole safer for patients than synthetic molecules.
Copying a venom peptide exactly is the surest route to an approved drug.

proof.quote: Chemists did not develop the peptide
built a small molecule that met it the same way and could be swallowed
hits the same target with a synthetic molecule of similar shape
most of them injected

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the chemists did not develop the pit viper peptide but built a small molecule that met the enzyme the same way, and tirofiban does the same at the platelet target, so the venom supplied the model rather than the product.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10 says most of the approved drugs are injected.
Tirofiban aims at the same target as the peptide-based drug beside it, so the two are not reaching different places.
Paragraph 7 gives venom peptides narrow windows and paragraph 11 lists the trouble they bring, so the passage does not treat them as the safer option.
Paragraph 8 makes the opposite point, since the chemists set the peptide aside and built something that could be swallowed.

questions.stem: Paragraph 12 suggests that after a peptide has been closed into a ring to protect it from enzymes, a researcher would most likely have to
choices: raise the dose to make up for the potency lost in the change
set the molecule aside, since a closed ring cannot bind a channel
repeat the gland sequencing to confirm the change was made
check whether it still tells its target from related proteins
move the drug from injection to some form taken by mouth

proof.quote: alters the surface that made the peptide selective
the rebuilt molecule often has to prove itself again

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says each such change alters the surface that made the peptide selective, so the rebuilt molecule has to prove itself again, and paragraph 4 explains that this surface is what does the discriminating.
distractorNotes: Lost potency is not what paragraph 12 warns about; the risk it names is lost selectivity.
That goes well past the passage, which presents ring closure as a tool that works and carries a cost worth checking.
Sequencing in paragraph 14 is a way of learning what an animal makes, not a way of confirming a chemical modification.
Nothing in paragraph 12 promises that these changes let a peptide survive the gut, and paragraph 11 names more than one obstacle there.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Venom research has absorbed decades of effort and should now give way to other approaches.
The chief obstacle to venom-derived medicine has always been the difficulty of collecting enough raw venom to work with.
Cone snails and spiders offer the most promising starting points for the drugs of the future.
Venom peptides matter chiefly because they showed that ion channels come in many related forms.
Venom offers unusually selective molecules, yet the gap between potency and medicine keeps the drug list short.

proof.quote: The premise is sound.
The output is thin.
Binding tightly to a human channel is a laboratory result, not a therapy
The gap between a peptide that exists and one that can be given to a patient
The bottleneck moved rather than vanished.

questions.why: The passage moves from why venom peptides are so selective, through why potency alone does not make a drug, to the short list of approvals and the reasons behind it, which is what this choice says.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 16 refuses that dismissal and credits venom with real drugs and a larger number of research tools.
Paragraph 14 says supply was the old limit and that gland sequencing removed it, so the current bottleneck lies elsewhere.
Cone snails and spiders appear as examples, and the passage never ranks sources by how promising they are.
Paragraph 16 gives research tools a supporting role, and the point there is that a peptide proves what a subtype does.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in describing ziconotide at length is to
choices: show a peptide that works as intended and is still barely usable
argue that opioids ought to be replaced with peptides wherever that is possible
demonstrate that cone snail venom is the most potent venom yet measured
illustrate how quickly gland sequencing can turn a peptide into a medicine
explain why disulfide bonds leave a peptide too rigid to act on a channel

proof.quote: it eases pain when opioids have failed
It is also close to unusable.
Captopril is the template, not ziconotide.

questions.why: Paragraph 9 grants that the drug eases pain when opioids have failed, then lists everything that makes it close to unusable, which makes it the clearest case of the gap the passage is built around.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9 mentions opioids only to say who the drug is for, and it makes no recommendation about replacing them.
The passage never ranks venoms by strength, and potency is not why this drug is featured.
Gland sequencing belongs to paragraph 14, and ziconotide is presented as a problem case rather than a quick success.
Paragraph 3 presents disulfide bonds as what makes a peptide durable, and ziconotide blocks its channel perfectly well.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: A history of one drug, followed by predictions about several others to come
A popular claim, the biology behind it, the obstacles and the record, a revised verdict
A list of unsolved problems, each paired with a solution already in use today
A comparison of two competing schools of thought, with the evidence for each weighed in turn

questions.why: Paragraph 1 opens with the familiar claim, paragraphs 2 through 5 explain why the peptides are so selective, the middle paragraphs turn to what stands in the way and what has actually been approved, and paragraph 16 delivers a reworked judgment.
distractorNotes: Captopril and ziconotide are examples along the way, and the passage makes no predictions about drugs to come.
Paragraph 12 does pair tools with problems, but that is one paragraph, and most of what the passage raises goes unsolved.
No two camps are set against each other; the author is arguing with one widely repeated framing.
Methods appear only in paragraph 14, and the passage never tells researchers how to do their work.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that evolution has already screened venom for useful drugs is best described as
choices: openly contemptuous of the researchers who reach for the phrase
untroubled, since the phrase captures the situation well enough
bluntly skeptical of a phrase claiming more than it earns
puzzled by a comparison whose meaning is difficult to make out
enthusiastic about the promise the phrase is meant to convey

the framing that keeps the field oversold

questions.why: Paragraph 13 calls the metaphor a great deal of unearned work and says counting sequences is not counting leads, which is criticism of the phrase rather than of the science or the people using it.
distractorNotes: The criticism falls on the framing, not the people, and paragraph 16 credits the field with real results.
Paragraph 13 is built entirely on the objection that the phrase is misleading.
The author states plainly what the phrase implies and why that implication is wrong, so nothing here is unclear.
Paragraph 1 reports that enthusiasm as something other people express, and paragraph 13 pushes back against it.
